blocks.text: Romans 7 sharply distinguishes the law from sin. Although the commandment exposes coveting and becomes the occasion through which sin works death, the chapter calls the law holy, righteous, good, and spiritual. The problem, therefore, is not that the law itself is sin, but that sin exploits what is good.

The first-person account from verses 7–25 is a major interpretive question. Readers have understood the speaker as autobiographical, as representing Adam or Israel, as a rhetorical voice, or in other ways; the chapter itself does not settle the speaker’s identity or temporal standpoint. That uncertainty should remain visible when reading the struggle described here.

Sin is described as an active power: it finds an opportunity, deceives, kills, dwells within, wages war, and takes captive. This language should not collapse physical death, personal moral agency, and personified enslaving power into one idea, nor should it be treated as a psychiatric diagnosis.

This chapter’s critique of sin and its use of the law should not be read as portraying Torah or Judaism as uniquely legalistic. Romans continues to honor Israel’s Scriptures and gifts while locating sin and boasting across peoples.

In the surrounding discussion, “flesh” is context-sensitive. It should not be equated simply with the physical body, sexuality, disability, or matter as inherently evil. Likewise, the wider passages distinguish physical death, enslaving powers, ethical agency, resurrection, transformation, grief, arrival, and judgment; these categories should not be transferred uncritically from one passage to another.

sections.title: Flesh and Death in the Surrounding Argument
